query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy at elevated temperature, simultaneous mechanical wear disrupts the thermally and chemically modified protective oxide/passive film on the distinct constituent phases. This film removal repeatedly exposes less-resistant substrate regions that are then more rapidly corroded, which in turn compromises the ability to reform or maintain an effective passive barrier. The cycle of wear-induced film breakdown and consequent accelerated corrosion creates a synergistic degradation process that is more severe than the linear summation of the individual wear and corrosion effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a finely distributed eutectic microstructure that, under high temperature, forms an initially protective but thermally unstable passive oxide film on its constituent phases.
generation.intervention: Expose matched alloy specimens to controlled conditions: (a) mechanical wear only in an inert high-temperature atmosphere, (b) corrosion only in a high-temperature, chloride-containing corrosive environment, and (c) simultaneous wear and corrosion under identical high-temperature and mechanical load conditions. In addition, compare results to a baseline monophase HEA of similar composition that does not develop the same eutectic microstructure.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., >600°C) with controlled corrosive medium (e.g., chloride/sulfuric acid mixture), and well-defined mechanical loads typical of sliding or abrasive wear.
generation.structural_mediator: The stability and integrity of the protective oxide/passive film on the eutectic phases.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear removes or deteriorates the modified protective oxide film. This exposes underlying metal phases that are inherently more susceptible to corrosion because the local environment (enhanced by temperature-induced defect formation in the oxide) accelerates electrochemical degradation. The resulting corrosion further disrupts the film formation, initiating a positive feedback loop that drives the coupled degradation process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the total degradation rate will be significantly greater than the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion responses. Specifically, both the wear rate (due to accelerated removal of the protective film and exposure of softer, corroded material) and the corrosion rate (due to continuous exposure of reactive substrate) will be increased relative to the baseline monophase alloy and to conditions where either wear or corrosion acts alone.
generation.baseline: A matched monophase HEA with similar overall composition but lacking the eutectic microstructure and the related two-phase protective film formation, as well as results from isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests on the eutectic alloy.
generation.boundary: Testing must be conducted under high-temperature conditions (e.g., >600°C) in a controlled corrosive medium (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid) while maintaining identical mechanical loads across comparisons. The physical and chemical environments must be maintained constant, aside from the specific intervention (wear, corrosion, or both), to ensure valid comparisons.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative enhancement of the coupled degradation over the sum of isolated effects is uncertain, as is the relative contribution of microstructural heterogeneity to local film stability. The magnitude of the acceleration might vary with precise temperature, loading conditions, and corrosion species concentrations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical multi‐phase eutectic HEA samples and subject them to three conditions: (1) wear only in an inert high-temperature setup; (2) corrosion only in the designated corrosive medium at the same temperature; and (3) combined wear and corrosion under identical temperature and load. Additionally, include control tests using a matched monophase HEA. Compare the total degradation rates (material loss, microstructural damage) and separate wear and corrosion contributions measured over time.
measurements: Surface profilometry (to quantify wear track depth/volume)
Electrochemical corrosion rate (via Tafel analysis or impedance spectroscopy)
Surface analysis (XPS/SEM) to monitor oxide film integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation observed in the combined wear and corrosion tests does not significantly exceed the sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only cases, or if the modification of the corrosive environment (e.g., lowering chloride concentration) does not result in the predicted modulation of degradation rates, then the hypothesis that wear-induced protective film breakdown accelerates overall degradation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. frame.goal: To elucidate and validate a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains the acceleration of degradation when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously at elevated temperature, and to predict the relative effects on overall degradation as well as the individual wear and corrosion responses compared to a matched baseline.
frame.limitation: The current lack of a unified mechanistic explanation for how and why wear and corrosion mutually accelerate each other in a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy under high-temperature conditions.
constraints: Must provide a controlled comparison against a matched baseline alloy
Explanation must include predicted changes in total degradation and separated contributions of wear and corrosion
Relevant boundary conditions (mechanical load, temperature, corrosive environment) must be clearly defined
Supporting evidence and a clear falsification criterion are required

decision.trend: Early HEA investigations typically addressed wear and corrosion as separate degradation channels. For instance, PMC7515071 established that high-temperature wear could lead to the formation of protective oxide films, while PMC9319277 showed that elevated temperature destabilizes the passive film in eutectic HEAs under corrosive conditions. PMC7866258, meanwhile, linked phase evolution during processing to both wear and corrosion performance. Together, these works indicate that while each process can be beneficially managed in isolation, their simultaneous occurrence leads to a dynamic interplay where mechanical removal (or alteration) of the protective film by wear exposes reactive substrates that enhance corrosion, and vice versa.
decision.unsolved: A unified mechanistic hypothesis that explains the coupling—that is, how the mechanically induced breakdown of a thermally and chemically modified protective oxide/passive film accelerates overall degradation in eutectic HEAs under simultaneous wear and corrosion at high temperature—remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Design a comparative study where identical eutectic HEA samples are exposed to three controlled conditions: (a) wear only in an inert high-temperature environment, (b) corrosion only in a high-temperature, corrosive medium, and (c) simultaneous wear and corrosion under the same high-temperature and mechanical load conditions. The key parameter lever is the controlled modification of the corrosive environment (e.g., chloride concentration and oxygen partial pressure) while maintaining matched mechanical loads and temperatures, and comparing the response against a baseline alloy (e.g., a monophase HEA with similar composition but without the eutectic microstructure).
decision.why: This approach allows one to isolate the role of wear-induced protective film removal and its subsequent effect on corrosion rates. It directly tests the hypothesis that the accelerated degradation is governed by the instability of the oxide/passive layers under simultaneous mechanical and chemical attack—a trend that emerges from prior studies but was never studied under strictly controlled comparative conditions. The clear falsification criterion would be if the coupled degradation does not exceed the sum of individual wear and corrosion contributions relative to the matched baseline, or if altering the environment (e.g., reducing corrosive species) fails to modulate the degradation rate as predicted.
